steps.action: Perform time-out: verify patient identity, procedure, allergies, and anticoagulation status.
steps.safety: Caudal approach avoids direct needle contact with thecal sac but has higher infection risk due to proximity to the sacral hiatus.
steps.teaching: The caudal approach enters the epidural space through the sacral hiatus. It is useful for bilateral lower lumbar and sacral pathology, and in patients with prior lumbar surgery.

steps.action: Review imaging. Palpate the sacral hiatus to assess anatomy. Note any pilonidal cyst or skin abnormalities.
steps.safety: Avoid the procedure if there is active skin infection near the sacral hiatus or pilonidal disease.
steps.teaching: The sacral hiatus is formed by the unfused S5 (and sometimes S4) laminae. The sacral cornua are palpable landmarks flanking the hiatus.

steps.action: Position patient prone with pillow under the pelvis to flex the hips and expose the sacral hiatus.
steps.safety: Ensure sterile prep extends widely around the gluteal cleft. This area has higher bacterial colonization.
steps.teaching: Hip flexion tilts the pelvis and makes the sacral hiatus more prominent. The hiatus is located approximately at the level of the posterior superior iliac spines.

steps.action: Obtain lateral fluoroscopic view to visualize the sacral canal and hiatus. Identify the sacral cornua.
steps.safety: Lateral view is the primary working view for caudal epidurals. Confirm the needle trajectory is within the sacral canal.
steps.teaching: On lateral fluoroscopy, the sacral canal appears as a lucent line between the dorsal and ventral sacral plates. The sacrococcygeal membrane covers the hiatus.

steps.action: Select a 22-gauge spinal needle or 20-gauge short-bevel needle. Insert through the sacrococcygeal membrane at ~45-degree angle, then flatten to advance into the sacral canal.
steps.safety: Initial steep angle penetrates the membrane, then flatten to avoid penetrating the ventral sacral plate. Advance only 1-2 cm past the membrane.
steps.teaching: The sacrococcygeal membrane gives a characteristic 'pop' or 'give' upon puncture. Over-advancement risks anterior dural puncture or penetration into the presacral space.

steps.action: Confirm needle position on AP view (midline within the sacral canal) and lateral view (within the sacral canal, below the S3 level).
steps.safety: The thecal sac typically ends at S2. Do not advance the needle above the S3 level to avoid dural puncture.
steps.teaching: In adults, the thecal sac ends at approximately the S2 level. In some individuals, it may extend to S3. Keeping the needle below S3 provides a safety margin.

steps.action: Inject 2-3 mL of contrast under live fluoroscopy. Confirm epidural spread pattern ascending the sacral canal.
steps.safety: Absence of epidural spread suggests subcutaneous or presacral placement. If contrast outlines individual nerve roots (myelogram pattern), needle is intrathecal.
steps.teaching: Caudal epidural contrast typically shows a linear, smooth pattern ascending the sacral canal, often with a 'railroad track' appearance on AP view.

steps.action: Inject injectate: 6-10 mL total volume including steroid (triamcinolone 80 mg or dexamethasone 10 mg) and preservative-free normal saline.
steps.safety: Larger volumes are needed for caudal to reach the lower lumbar epidural space. Inject slowly to avoid excessive pressure.
steps.teaching: The caudal approach requires larger volumes (6-10 mL) compared to interlaminar (2-3 mL) or transforaminal (1.5-2 mL) because the injectate must traverse the sacral canal to reach the target level.

steps.action: Remove needle and apply sterile bandage. Monitor for 20-30 minutes.
steps.safety: Assess lower extremity strength and sensation. Larger injectate volumes may cause temporary motor block.
steps.teaching: Transient lower extremity weakness or numbness is more common after caudal injections due to the larger volumes bathing the sacral nerve roots.

steps.action: Document procedure details: needle type, fluoroscopic confirmation, contrast pattern, injectate volume and composition.
steps.safety: Document the level of contrast spread (which vertebral levels were covered) to guide future treatment decisions.
steps.teaching: If contrast does not reach the target level, the procedure may have reduced efficacy. Documentation helps guide repeat procedure planning.
